about.title: Fillmore Wrongful Death Claims
about.longDescription: When someone dies because another person was careless, the questions arrive quietly and all at once. How does the household keep going? In Fillmore, a Ventura County town of about 15,500 people, a loss like this is felt on every block, and the two traffic deaths recorded here in 2025 were not statistics to the families who lived through them. Many of the collisions logged in town cluster along Route 126 where it runs as Ventura Street, and on A Street. California law allows a surviving spouse or domestic partner and children to bring a wrongful death claim first, with certain dependents and heirs able to step in when they are not present. The claim is civil and moves separately from any criminal case, and it generally must be filed within two years of the death, sooner if a public agency is involved. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We listen, then connect you with an independent attorney who handles these cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: My family member was killed in a crash on Route 126 in Fillmore and the other driver faces charges. Do we still need a civil claim?
items.answer: Yes, the two proceed on separate tracks. A criminal case is brought by the Ventura County prosecutor and is about punishment, not about compensating your family. A wrongful death claim is a civil action you control, and it can move forward whether or not charges are filed or result in a conviction.

items.question: Who in our family is allowed to file a wrongful death claim in California?
items.answer: The surviving spouse or registered domestic partner and the children have the first right to bring the claim. If there is no spouse, partner or child, certain financially dependent relatives and legal heirs may qualify instead. An attorney can review your family situation and explain who should be named.

items.question: How much time do we have, and what can be recovered?
items.answer: In most cases the deadline is two years from the date of death, but if a government entity may be responsible, the first required step comes much sooner. Recoverable losses include funeral and burial expenses, the income and support your loved one would have contributed, and the loss of companionship, love and guidance. LawProactive can connect you with an independent attorney at no charge to review these questions.
